Morgan Stanley's Yeshaya said that transactions may come back when companies are more comfortable with new valuations. The IPO window has also narrowed, with [USN:L4N45U1C2 TEXT:"biotech"] among the few sectors still drawing interest as investors become more selective in a higher-rate environment. "In terms of the pipeline, equity markets is more follow-on driven. The IPO market continues to be a bit more selective, so certainly an option for issuers with durable earnings," Citigroup's Fraser said. IPOs typically require stable investor appetite and supportive market conditions for companies to achieve their desired valuations. Higher inflation and rising rates also make growth stocks look more expensive and increase the cost of debt. "Taking a step back, anyone with high expectations will be disappointed by Q4's IPO activity. To some extent that's true of 2026 as a whole," said Matt Kennedy, senior strategist at Renaissance Capital, a provider of IPO-focused research and ETFs. "Companies are still filing. Admittedly, that can change, and rising rates are new and meaningful headwinds. An end to the Iran war would be the largest potential catalyst to the upside, but that's impossible to predict."

item.title: Jury returns mixed verdict in Tyreek Hill's battery case
item.description: Free agent wideout Tyreek Hill was found liable for two counts of battery in a mixed verdict at his civil trial in Miami.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Free agent wideout Tyreek Hill was found liable for two counts of battery in a mixed verdict at his civil trial in Miami. The jury awarded $500,000 in compensatory damages to his estranged wife, Lakeeta Vaccaro. However, they found the NFL veteran not liable on eight other claims and denied Vaccaro's request for punitive damages. Hill, 32, who has been seeking a comeback after missing most of last season with a torn ACL, smiled and shook hands with his attorneys after the verdicts were read. "Mr. Hill was very pleased that he was able to get his story out and to be able to tell the world what he's not been able to speak about," attorney Christi Bright told reporters. "He's very grateful." After a weeklong trial, the six-person jury found Hill liable for an incident that occurred in January 2024 and another that took place on April 7, 2025, the day before she filed for divorce. Drew Rosenhaus, Hill's agent, said on Oct. 2 that his client was negotiating with teams and could sign later that week. Reported potential landing spots include his former team, the Kansas City Chiefs. Hill also posted cryptically on social media that he was "ready for some cold weather." "Nothing is imminent at this time," Rosenhaus told ESPN on Wednesday. "He's continuing his rehab with the goal of being on a team in the immediate future." Some of the testimony during his civil trial could potentially complicate a return to the NFL for the eight-time Pro Bowler. Vaccaro testified about a tumultuous relationship and alleged that Hill pulled her hair, knocked her to the ground, twisted her breasts and issued threats. Hill denied most of the allegations, although he admitted telling her during one argument that he could "get people to hurt her." A five-time first-team All-Pro, Hill was drafted in the fifth round by the Chiefs in 2016. After six successful seasons in Kansas City, he was traded to the Miami Dolphins before the 2022 season. Hill has 819 catches for 11,363 yards and 83 touchdowns in 145 games (127 starts) over 10 seasons. He topped 1,000 receiving yards six times, including a league-high 1,799 in 2023. --Field Level Media

item.title: OpenAI employee who left for Apple took files about unreleased device, OpenAI alleges
item.description: An OpenAI employee who left the ChatGPT maker for Apple sent more than 100 files about an unreleased product to a personal account and later made a presentation about the unreleased product to senior Apple leadership, a new filing in the lawsuit between OpenAI and Apple alleges.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Nellis, Deepa Seetharaman
item.content:encoded: An OpenAI employee who left the ChatGPT maker for Apple (AAPL.O) sent more than 100 files about an unreleased product to a personal account and later made a presentation about the unreleased product to senior Apple leadership, a new filing in the lawsuit between OpenAI and Apple alleges. In the filing in US federal court in San Jose, California, OpenAI alleged that the presentation happened months ago and that Apple is now making AI products of its own, citing the release of Apple's [USN:L6N45Y122 TEXT:"HomeView product this week"]. "OpenAI is very concerned that its trade secret and confidential information is now circulating inside Apple, where Apple engineers can shape Apple’s upcoming products based on OpenAI’s confidential and innovative work," OpenAI said in its filing. Apple said that it has policies and procedures in place to ensure new employees do not use confidential information from previous employers and that it has found no evidence to support OpenAI's allegations. The document, filed on Tuesday, is part of an [USN:L4N43C1AC TEXT:"ongoing trade secret dispute"] filed by Apple earlier this year in which it alleged employees of the iPhone maker left and took confidential information to OpenAI's hardware division. OpenAI has denied those allegations. Earlier this week, US District Court Judge Edward Davila granted part of Apple's request to get early access to digital files from OpenAI in the suit. Davila said Apple could gather data from some of its former employees' devices and sit three of them for depositions on a sped-up schedule, including the two defendants in the case — Chang Liu, a former senior system electrical engineer, and Tang Yew Tan, a former vice president of product design for iPhone and Apple Watch. The case is likely to go to trial in October 2027, though OpenAI has said in court filings that it could be ready for trial as soon as June 2027.

item.title: Perrigo to pay $10 million to settle US class action over baby formula prices
item.description: Perrigo has agreed to pay $10 million to settle a proposed class action alleging it conspired with Gerber Products to block new entrants into the market for store-brand infant formula, allowing Perrigo to inflate prices that retailers passed on to consumers.
item.dc:creator: Mike Scarcella
item.content:encoded: Perrigo (PRGO.N) has agreed to pay $10 million to settle a proposed class action alleging it conspired with Gerber Products to block new entrants into the market for store-brand infant formula, allowing Perrigo to inflate prices that retailers passed on to consumers. Here are the details: The consumer plaintiffs filed their proposed settlement with Perrigo in federal court in Brooklyn on Tuesday. The accord requires a judge’s approval The settlement covers customers of store-brand infant formula manufactured or sold by Perrigo since April 2020. The plaintiffs’ lawyers estimate there are millions of class members across the US Perrigo is a top supplier in the US of store-brand formula, which is sold under a retailer’s label and can cost less than similar branded products The settlement said Perrigo, which denied wrongdoing, will cooperate with the plaintiffs in their ongoing lawsuit against Gerber, including by making its directors, officers and employees available to testify and handing over transaction data Perrigo and Gerber did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Gerber also has denied any wrongdoing Under the deal, Perrigo will refrain for three years from making agreements with infant formula businesses that limit competition for store-brand formula without a legitimate business reason The case is Thomas Conry et al v. Gerber Products et al, US District Court for the Eastern District of New York, No. 1:24-cv-06784-NG-AYS. For plaintiffs: Jeffrey J. Corrigan of Spector Roseman & Kodroff and Simon Paris of Saltz Mongeluzzi For Perrigo: C. Scott Lent of Arnold & Porter Kaye Scholer

item.title: Six Kings Slam in Saudi Arabia postponed, AFC open to Asian Cup switch to 2028
item.description: The "Six Kings Slam" tennis tournament originally scheduled for October has been postponed to December 27–30, organisers said on Wednesday after the recent attacks on the kingdom while the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) is open to postponing the Asian Cup to 2028.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The "Six Kings Slam" tennis tournament originally scheduled for October has been postponed to December 27–30, organisers said on Wednesday after the recent attacks on the kingdom while the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) is open to postponing the Asian Cup to 2028. A strike on Riyadh's international airport on Saturday [USN:L1N45W03M TEXT:"killed at least 12 people"] and wounded more than 300, with Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement claiming responsibility for the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. "The decision reflects Riyadh Season's commitment to delivering sporting events to the highest standards, following an assessment of the organizational and logistical challenges associated with hosting the tournament and their potential impact on the quality of the audience experience," organisers said in a statement. Carlos Alcaraz, Novak Djokovic, Alexander Zverev and Taylor Fritz were set to take part in the event from October 21-24. Defending champion Jannik Sinner withdrew due to injury. The tournament is an exhibition event which draws the world's top players due to the record prize money on offer, with Alcaraz acknowledging in 2024 that the financial aspect played a role as he earned $1.5 million over four days. The attacks have threatened to disrupt sport in the kingdom, with [USN:L4N45Z0SF TEXT:"golf's Asian Tour"] also saying it is monitoring the security situation ahead of the Saudi International in Riyadh next month. AFC IN 'NO HURRY' TO MAKE DECISION Saudi Arabia is also set to stage the Asian Cup in soccer for the first time in 2027, a key test ahead of the kingdom's hosting of the 2034 World Cup. The 24-team tournament is scheduled to kick off on January 7 across eight venues in three cities - Riyadh, Jeddah and Al-Khobar. AFC president Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa said they were in "no hurry to make a decision" on whether to postpone the tournament or not. "We can wait until the end of November. Things can change very quickly for better or worse in the region and it is question of seeing what happens," he told reporters in Zurich where the FIFA Council is meeting. "If we need to make a decision then we will, but we could move back a year to 2028 if we need to. But at the moment we are monitoring the situation and everything is on schedule." The 2023 tournament was postponed from June 2023 to July 2024 after China withdrew as hosts due to COVID-19 restrictions and Qatar stepped in to host the tournament in the winter. Saudi Arabia is also hosting the FIFAe World Cup, an esports tournament series held by world soccer's governing body FIFA, in Jeddah from October 16-25. However, the Japan Football Association said it would not participate following a comprehensive assessment of the current situation in the host country and the available information regarding safety and security. Football Australia also said its security team was monitoring the situation. Reuters has contacted the AFC and FIFA for comment.

item.title: Apple asks US court to overturn jury's landmark $5.7 billion patent verdict
item.description: Apple has asked a federal judge in San Diego to overturn a $5.7 billion patent verdict won by Taction Technology against the tech giant last month over the haptic feedback in Apple's iPhones and Apple Watches.
item.dc:creator: Blake Brittain
item.content:encoded: Apple (AAPL.O) has asked a federal judge in San Diego to overturn a $5.7 billion patent verdict won by Taction Technology against the tech giant last month over the haptic feedback in Apple's iPhones and Apple Watches. Apple told the court on Tuesday that the verdict, the largest patent verdict in US history by more than $3 billion, was "untethered to any evidence at all" Spokespeople and attorneys for Taction did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday San Diego-based Taction, which uses its haptic technology in headphones and gaming headsets, filed the lawsuit in 2021 A jury [USN:L6N45I048 TEXT:"determined"] on September 25 that Apple's Taptic Engine, which creates tapping vibrations, infringed two Taction patents Apple told the court on Tuesday that there was insufficient evidence to support the award, and said that US District Judge Todd Robinson told the companies' attorneys before the verdict was read that he was "not sure that the figure that appears on the verdict form is what the jury meant to convey" Several other US patent verdicts worth more than $1 billion [USN:L1N2TK0T8 TEXT:"have been"] [USN:L1N3CZ18G TEXT:"overturned"] or reduced in the past The case is Taction Technology v. Apple Inc, US District Court for the Southern District of California, No. 3:21-cv-00812 For Taction: Lance Yang of Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan For Apple: Roger Denning of Fish & Richardson Read more: [USN:L6N45I048 TEXT:"US jury says Apple owes record $5.7 billion in haptic technology patent case"]

item.title: Banks, buildings burn as Albania's capital Tirana erupts into student violence
item.description: Tens of thousands of students stormed the streets of Tirana on Wednesday, setting alight a government building and two banks and hurling stones at police during a protest over rising education costs and corruption.
item.dc:creator: Fatos Bytyci
item.content:encoded: Tens of thousands of students stormed the streets of Tirana on Wednesday, setting alight a government building and two banks and hurling stones at police during a protest over rising education costs and corruption. Police responded with water cannons and tear gas to disperse protesters who started a fire at the ministry of education building, overturned garbage cans and smashed the fronts of local businesses, Reuters footage showed. A Raiffeisen Bank branch near the education ministry also caught fire, a Reuters witness said. The protests represent the most violent outburst against Prime Minister Edi Rama, who won a fourth term in office in elections in May last year but has since faced growing discontent at [USN:L6N3ZC0BA TEXT:"perceived graft"] surrounding top officials. Protesters also dismiss opposition figures as unpalatable alternatives. The unrest caps a summer of peaceful protests against Rama, triggered by the proposed development of a [USN:L6N4380FB TEXT:"luxury resort"] along Albania's pristine southern coast backed by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner which has been [USN:L6N42J18T TEXT:"caught up in legal disputes"]. "This is a revolution. We are tired of peaceful protests. We will not stop until Rama resigns," said Lora, a student who declined to give her last name said as she threw rocks at the police. Others chanted "Resignation" and "Police of crime." WIDER PROTESTS Student organisers said the protest was over conditions at universities, higher education costs, a lack of financial support and employment prospects after graduation. The unrest is part of a broader wave of student activism sweeping Europe over education and living conditions. In France, high school students have staged [USN:L1N45U08J TEXT:"weeks of protests"] and school blockades demanding more teachers and better facilities, arguing that deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms are undermining education. Albanian media reported that Wednesday's protests spread to universities at Elbasan and Shkodra. The government condemned the violence. "Protesting is a legitimate right, but it cannot be used as an excuse for violence, city destruction or ugly fighting in the middle of the road," Deputy Prime Minister Albana Kociu said on Facebook. "I call on students and every honest citizen who believes in the right to protest: Distance yourself from violence and vandalism!" The police issued a statement calling for calm. "Any person who uses violence, burns or destroys property, or attacks Police officers, bears individual responsibility and will face the law, in accordance with the offences committed," it said.

item.title: Kazakhstan-linked hackers targeted Russian refinery, spied on city government, researchers say
item.description: Hackers likely based in Kazakhstan targeted a Russian oil refinery and compromised a Russian municipal government network earlier this year, researchers said on Wednesday, a rare glimpse of cyberespionage being deployed against Moscow from a smaller neighbour.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Satter
item.content:encoded: Hackers likely based in Kazakhstan targeted a Russian oil refinery and compromised a Russian municipal government network earlier this year, researchers said on Wednesday, a rare glimpse of cyberespionage being deployed against Moscow from a smaller neighbour. In a joint report , Chi-en Shen from Cisco (CSCO.O) and Julian-Ferdinand Vögele of the cybersecurity firm Recorded Future said the hackers -- nicknamed "Silent Lynx" -- were "likely based in Kazakhstan" and had hacked into government organizations across Central Asia. The researchers said Silent Lynx favoured “spear phishing” emails, using important-looking attachments to infect targets unwary enough to open them. The spying was "a reminder that the cyberespionage game is not limited to only a few cyber powers," said Oleg Shakirov, a doctoral student who studies cyber policy and conflict at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies. "Other nations are catching up." The researchers said Silent Lynx targeted the Orsk Oil Refinery in southern Russia, [USN:S8N42X012 TEXT:"which was knocked out for months"] after it was hit in a Ukrainian drone attack in August, and that there was evidence they had broken into the government of Nizhny Novgorod, a city about 425 kilometers (265 miles) east of Moscow. The mid-sized Orsknefteorgsintez refinery is about 25 kilometers (16 miles) from the Kazakh border; repeated outages from Ukrainian drone attacks have prompted the Russian government to [USN:S8N3MT07U TEXT:"tap Kazakhstan for refining capacity"]. Nizhny Novgorod sits at the confluence of the Volga and Oka rivers and is upstream of the Caspian Sea, a critical body of water for landlocked Kazakhstan. The Orsk refinery and Nizhny Novgorod government did not return messages seeking comment. Attempts to reach the hackers were unsuccessful. The researchers said evidence for Silent Lynx's Kazakh ties included apparent efforts by the hackers to test their malicious software from Kazakhstan shortly after its code was compiled and activity consistent with Kazakh working hours. The hackers' spy campaign also lined up with Kazakhstan's strategic interests, the researchers said. For example, they said they found evidence that the hackers had compromised a Tajik government agency just as Kazakhstan was ratifying a treaty with Tajikistan in early 2026, as well as evidence that a Belarusian government agency was similarly compromised ahead of a meeting between diplomats from Belarus and Kazakhstan in April. The Kazakh, Russian, Tajik and Belarusian governments did not return messages seeking comment.

item.title: Dois navios afundam perto de Ormuz após serem atingidos por projéteis em meio a onda de ataques
item.description: Um navio porta-contêineres e um navio graneleiro afundaram perto do Estreito de Ormuz nas últimas 24 horas, após serem atingidos por projéteis em incidentes separados, informaram autoridades marítimas nesta quarta-feira.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Um navio porta-contêineres e um navio graneleiro afundaram perto do Estreito de Ormuz nas últimas 24 horas, após serem atingidos por projéteis em incidentes separados, informaram autoridades marítimas nesta quarta-feira. Os ataques na região da via navegável aumentaram nos últimos 10 dias. O Irã afirma estar intensificando as ações em resposta ao bloqueio de seus portos pelos EUA e às sanções mais rigorosas impostas no mês passado. O GFS Pride, um navio porta-contêineres de pequeno porte com bandeira de Cingapura e capacidade para 2.824 unidades equivalentes a 20 pés (TEU), afundou enquanto navegava pelo estreito, segundo fontes de segurança marítima. "O GFS Pride sofreu danos e um incêndio a bordo, vindo a afundar posteriormente. Todos os 21 tripulantes foram retirados em segurança. Não houve relatos de feridos", informou a Autoridade Marítima e Portuária de Cingapura (MPA) em um comunicado na quarta-feira, acrescentando que a embarcação navegava pelo estreito na terça-feira. Em um incidente separado, o Cape Dao, com bandeira de Antígua e Barbuda, afundou nas proximidades do estreito, semanas após ter sido atingido por um projétil em 23 de setembro, segundo dados divulgados na quarta-feira pela Organização Marítima Internacional (OMI), agência da ONU para o setor de navegação. Um tripulante morreu e o restante da tripulação foi retirado logo após o ataque, informaram fontes marítimas. A empresa responsável pela gestão da embarcação, a Peonies Shipmanagement FZE, sediada nos Emirados Árabes Unidos, não pôde ser contatada imediatamente para comentar o caso. GFS Pride e Cape Dao são a segunda e a terceira embarcações a afundar desde o início do conflito entre EUA e Irã, em 28 de fevereiro, segundo uma análise de dados da OMI sobre incidentes marítimos. "A MPA está profundamente preocupada com os ataques contínuos à navegação comercial no Estreito de Ormuz", afirmou a autoridade de Cingapura. "Tais ataques são não provocados, injustificáveis e constituem uma violação do direito internacional." A empresa responsável pela gestão do GFS Pride, a GFS Ship Management FZE, sediada nos Emirados Árabes Unidos, não pôde ser contatada imediatamente para comentar o caso. "Os incidentes mais recentes reforçam a ameaça contínua à navegação comercial que transita pelo Estreito de Ormuz", afirmou na quarta-feira a Marisks, empresa de gestão de riscos marítimos. "A ameaça não se limita a navios-tanque. Navios porta-contêineres e graneleiros também têm sofrido danos graves." O Irã está empregando novas táticas para atacar navios que navegam pelo Estreito de Ormuz, na tentativa de manter os preços do petróleo elevados e influenciar as eleições de meio de mandato nos EUA, disseram duas autoridades iranianas de alto escalão à Reuters.

item.title: Sportradar hit by EU, UK antitrust complaints from rival
item.description: Sports technology company Sportradar Group was hit with antitrust complaints to EU and UK regulators on Wednesday by sportsbook software company Altenar Technologies, which accused it of blocking rivals' access to its live official sports data.
item.dc:creator: Yun Chee Foo
item.content:encoded: Sports technology company Sportradar Group (1M4.F) was hit with antitrust complaints to EU and UK regulators on Wednesday by sportsbook software company Altenar Technologies, which accused it of blocking rivals' access to its live official sports data. Swiss-headquartered Sportradar is a leading content provider of betting-related content in major sports including tennis, soccer and basketball. Its exclusive deals with major sports leagues MLB, NBA, ATP, and NHL include data collection and distribution rights, as well as the right to provide live betting odds derived from that data. "We have received information on this matter, which we are assessing," said a spokesperson for the European Commission, commenting on the situation. The complaints follow an antitrust lawsuit Altenar filed in a US court in April, alleging Sportradar has monopolised the market for live official sports data in the US and stifled competition. Sportradar said it was aware of Altenar's February 2026 threats to file complaints with competition authorities in multiple jurisdictions. "Altenar's latest efforts to inflame the news agenda appear duplicative, unnecessary and serve as a thinly veiled attempt to assert pressure in the existing commercial disputes in process. Sportradar has and will continue to comply with antitrust and other laws wherever it does business," a Sportradar spokesperson said. Britain's Competition and Markets Authority said it did not comment on specific examples or scenarios outside of a formal investigation. "We believe Sportradar is using its control of essential sports data to shut out businesses with a competing offer," an Altenar spokesperson said. "Bookmakers across the EU and UK need a choice of suppliers and a market that supports competition and innovation. We are asking the European Commission and the CMA to intervene and ensure that independent providers can compete on fair terms," the spokesperson said. Altenar is also asking the CMA to impose interim measures restoring access to essential data and odds pending the outcome of an investigation. EU antitrust violations can result in fines of up to 10% of a company's annual global turnover.

item.title: Two ships sink near Hormuz after being hit by projectiles amid surge in attacks
item.description: A container ship and a dry bulk carrier have both sunk near the Strait of Hormuz in the past 24 hours after being hit by projectiles in separate incidents, maritime officials said on Wednesday.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Saul, Renee Maltezou
item.content:encoded: A container ship and a dry bulk carrier have both sunk near the Strait of Hormuz in the past 24 hours after being hit by projectiles in separate incidents, maritime officials said on Wednesday. Attacks around the waterway [USN:L1N45U0E0 TEXT:"have surged over the past 10 days"], with Iran saying it is stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions introduced last month. The Singapore-flagged GFS Pride, a small container vessel with a capacity of 2,824 20-foot equivalent units (TEU), sank while sailing through the strait, according to maritime security sources. "GFS PRIDE sustained damage and a fire on board, and has since sunk. All 21 crew members were safely evacuated. No injuries have been reported," the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) said in a statement on Wednesday, adding that the vessel had been sailing through the strait on Tuesday. In a separate incident, the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao sank close to the strait, weeks after being struck by a projectile on September 23, data from UN shipping agency the International Maritime Organization showed on Wednesday. One crew member was killed, the rest of the crew evacuated straight after the strike, maritime sources said. Its UAE-based manager Peonies Shipmanagement FZE could not be immediately reached for comment. The GFS Pride and Cape Dao are the second and third vessels to have sunk since the US-Iran war began on February 28, according to an analysis of IMO casualty data. "MPA is deeply concerned about the continued attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz," the Singapore authority said. "Such attacks are unprovoked, unjustifiable, and a breach of international law." GFS Pride's United Arab Emirates-based manager, GFS Ship Management FZE, could not be immediately reached for comment. "The latest incidents reinforce the continuing threat to commercial shipping transiting the Strait of Hormuz," maritime risk management company MARISKS said on Wednesday. "The threat is not confined to tankers, with container vessels and bulk carriers also sustaining serious damage." IRAN TIGHTENS GRIP A sharp escalation in threats to commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade passed before the war, has heightened concerns about security in the waterway. Tehran has sought to tighten its grip on the waterway since US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, restricting transit in an effort to gain leverage over Washington. Iran is increasingly deploying new tactics against vessels transiting the strait as it seeks to keep oil prices elevated and influence US midterm elections, [USN:L8N45Z15J TEXT:"two senior Iranian officials told Reuters."] While Iran and the US have focused their attacks on tankers, cargo and container vessels have also been attacked, immobilised or sunk. The Maltese-flagged container ship Safeen Prestige was hit by a projectile in March and later sank north of the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's Revolutionary Guards attacked and seized the container ship MSC Francesca in April.

item.title: US inflation heats up in September; Fed rate hike this month back on table
item.description: US consumer prices accelerated in September as the cost of gasoline surged, dealing another blow to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party ahead of the November 3 midterm elections and putting an interest rate increase later this month back on the radar.
item.dc:creator: Lucia Mutikani
item.content:encoded: US consumer prices accelerated in September as the cost of gasoline surged, dealing another blow to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party ahead of the November 3 midterm elections and putting an interest rate increase later this month back on the radar. The Consumer Price Index report from the Labor Department on Wednesday showed a broadening of price pressures beyond energy, raising concerns among economists that underlying inflation could be getting sticky. There was also an AI-related boost to inflation last month. Financial markets now see the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision at its October 27-28 meeting as a closer call than before the data was released. The report added to surveys this month that showed a further deterioration in [USN:L1N45V0J1 TEXT:"consumer sentiment"] and a plunge in Trump's [USN:L6N45D0XN TEXT:"approval rating"], driven by angst over the rising cost of living. A Reuters/Ipsos poll showed about 78% of Americans [USN:L6N45T0W3 TEXT:"blamed Trump's"] policies, including tariffs and the Middle East conflict, for rising prices, which are outpacing wages. "The inflation we're experiencing right now is largely the result of erratic policy from the executive branch," said Kyle Moore, chief economist at the Century Foundation, a progressive think tank. "Worse still, the directionless war in Iran continues to disrupt global supply chains. This administration has also been wholly unwilling to moderate the pace of the AI and data-center buildout." The CPI rose 0.6% last month after climbing 0.4% in August, the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics said, in line with economists' expectations. In the 12 months through September, the CPI advanced 3.7% after rising 3.4% in August. A 9.1% surge in gasoline prices accounted for more than half of the increase in the CPI over the month. The US-Israeli war with Iran is driving up [USN:L1N46003I TEXT:"energy prices"]. Other motor fuels, which include diesel, soared 11.9% last month and were up 60.9% on a year-over-year basis. Diesel prices at the pump are at record highs, and there are fears that those costs will soon feed through to higher prices at the supermarket. Food prices were unchanged after gaining 0.1% in both July and August. Grocery store prices dipped 0.1% over the month as beef prices dropped 1.0% and the cost of dairy and related products eased 0.9%. Egg prices declined 1.3%. But prices for nonalcoholic beverages surged 0.9%, while fruits and vegetables cost 0.5% more, with banana prices shooting up 1.0%, in what could be early signs of rising trucking costs being passed on to consumers. Lettuce prices rebounded 3.9% as a cyclospora outbreak faded. Grocery prices rose 1.8% on a year-over-year basis. Average hourly earnings for all employees declined 0.7% in September from a year ago, after falling 0.3% in August, underscoring the squeeze on consumers in what economists call the bottom of a K-shaped economy. Economists said this data raised doubts about whether consumers could maintain their robust pace of spending. "While much of the lost purchasing power is due to rising energy costs, there is no reason to expect that to fade in the near term," said Eric Winograd, chief US economist at AllianceBernstein. "The bottom part of the K-shaped economy is losing ground, as anybody who has seen campaign ads on TV the last few weeks has heard." With the cost of living rising, the Social Security Administration announced a [USN:L1N45Z0SL TEXT:"3.6% cost-of-living adjustment"] for Social Security and Supplemental Security Income benefits for 2027. The programs benefit nearly 72 million Americans, including retirees, the disabled and certain widows, widowers and children. Social Security retirement benefits will, on average, increase by $75 per month. Stocks on Wall Street fell. The dollar advanced versus a basket of currencies. Yields on US Treasury notes and bonds rose. Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the CPI rose 0.3% in September, matching the gain in August. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the so-called core CPI would increase 0.2%. The core CPI was lifted by a 0.4% advance in the cost of shelter, including hotel and motel rooms. Owners' equivalent rent, a measure of the amount homeowners would pay to rent or would earn from renting their property, rose 0.3%. Airline fares rose 1.2% amid higher jet fuel prices. Consumers paid more for gardening and lawn care services, likely reflecting worker shortages amid a crackdown on undocumented immigrants. The costs of recreation and education also rose, as did those of hospital and dental services. Overall services prices increased 0.4%. They were also up 0.4% excluding energy. Core goods prices rose 0.3%, pushed up by a 0.7% increase in the cost of used cars and trucks. Apparel prices climbed 0.3% and the cost of toys rebounded 4.2%, suggesting some lingering pass-through from tariffs. But prescription medication was cheaper. Prices for computers and peripherals jumped 1.3%, reflecting AI-related investment, while the cost of computer software and accessories rebounded 0.4%. In the 12 months through September, core CPI inflation was 2.6%, compared with 2.4% in August. The US central bank tracks the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index for its 2% inflation target. Financial markets raised the chances of a rate hike at the Fed's meeting this month to roughly 37% from about 22% prior to the release of the CPI report, CME Group's FedWatch Tool showed. The odds of a rate increase this month had diminished following [USN:L1N45N170 TEXT:"underwhelming payroll"] gains in September as well as cooler-than-expected PCE [USN:L1N45M0L0 TEXT:"inflation readings"] for July and August. The Fed in September raised its [USN:L6N4570XW TEXT:"overnight benchmark interest rate"] by 25 basis points to the 3.75%-4.00% range, its first hike in three years, and flagged further increases in borrowing costs in the months ahead. Most economists continue to expect the Fed will hold rates steady this month and raise them in December. Based on the CPI data, economists' estimates for core PCE inflation ranged from 0.3% to 0.4%, which would mean a year-over-year reading of 3.1%. Producer price data being released on Thursday could impact those estimates. Core PCE inflation was 0.2% in August and 3.0% on a year-over-year basis. "What is interesting is that the primary drivers of inflation are supply-side policies that are better addressed by the fiscal authority," said Joseph Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM. "However, that is not going to happen anytime soon, which leaves the Fed to address a re-establishment of price stability."

item.title: Japan to invest $21 billion in up to two GlobalFoundries chip factories in New York
item.description: Japan will invest about $21 billion to build up to two chip factories in New York State that will be jointly owned by the US government and Japanese interests and operated by GlobalFoundries , the company said on Wednesday.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Nellis, David Shepardson, Makiko Yamazaki
item.content:encoded: Japan will invest about $21 billion to build up to two chip factories in New York State that will be jointly owned by the US government and Japanese interests and operated by GlobalFoundries (GFS.O) , the company said on Wednesday. The initiative is part of a Trump administration deal struck last year for Japan to invest $550 billion in the US in return for the US lowering tariffs on Japanese cars and other imports from at least 25% to 15%. Shares of Malta, New York-based GlobalFoundries, which is majority-owned by Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund Mubadala Investment Co, rose more than 4% in afternoon trading. They have gained more than 39% this year. Construction of the first factory is scheduled to begin this year with chip production expected in 2029. GlobalFoundries executives said the partners will decide whether to build the second factory before the end of 2028. The first factory is expected to add annual US manufacturing capacity for about 900,000 300mm wafers when fully operational, ranking it among the larger US semiconductor manufacturing facilities, and create more than 1,000 factory jobs in New York. The US government previously held a 3% stake in GlobalFoundries. GlobalFoundries CEO Tim Breen told Reuters that will rise to 7%. Japan will provide all of the investment capital under the deal. US President Donald Trump said on Truth Social the US government, which provided $1.63 billion in grants to the company, values the 7% stake in the company at more than $2 billion. "We are the first administration ever to turn grants into money for America," Trump said. Breen told Reuters initial customers for the New York factories include Japan's Renesas Electronics (6723.T) and iPhone maker Apple (AAPL.O) . On a conference call with investors, executives said the new deal will generate fees for the company for at least 20 years. This revenue is expected to be $50 million next year, when the company will earn fees for managing construction of the first factory. GlobalFoundries will shift $955 million previously awarded by the US government to accelerate investments in silicon photonics, silicon-germanium chip material and advanced packaging at its existing chip factories in Malta, New York, and Burlington, Vermont. GlobalFoundries' Breen said that at least some of the capital investment by Japan will flow back to chip-manufacturing toolmakers such as Tokyo Electron (8035.T) and other Japanese firms that along with US rivals dominate the supply chain. "Obviously, we have a strong interest in the Japanese equipment suppliers to be part of it," Breen said. "We will be very open-minded, but we'll definitely engage very much with the Japanese ecosystem because they have great technologies." Japan has so far announced two batches of projects worth over $100 billion combined under the overall investment scheme. Under the arrangement with the US, Trump selects projects to be funded by Japan. Available free cash flows from investments will be [USN:L1N42R099 TEXT:"split evenly"] between the two countries until a specific allocation is reached, after which 90% will go to the US.

item.title: Liquidia surges as United Therapeutics settlement removes key litigation risk
item.description: Liquidia shares jumped 26% on Wednesday after it settled a years-long legal dispute with United Therapeutics over its lung disease drug, removing a major litigation risk for the drugmaker.
item.dc:creator: Siddhi Mahatole
item.content:encoded: Liquidia (LQDA.O) shares jumped 26% on Wednesday after it settled a years-long legal dispute with United Therapeutics (UTHR.O) over its lung disease drug, removing a major litigation risk for the drugmaker. The settlement, announced late on Tuesday, ends six lawsuits over patents, trade secrets, contracts and antitrust claims related to Liquidia's Yutrepia, an inhaled dry-powder form of the drug treprostinil. "The agreement avoids more negative scenarios that had previously been priced in for Liquidia shares," said Needham analyst Serge Belanger. The drugmaker's shares had lost [USN:L4N45M1L4 TEXT:"more than half"] their value after an adverse court ruling last month. Yutrepia is approved to treat pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and pulmonary hypertension linked to interstitial lung disease (PH-ILD), and competes in the market with United Therapeutics' Tyvaso. As part of the settlement, Liquidia will stop promoting its drug for PH-ILD, but will keep selling it for PAH. It will also pay United Therapeutics about $380.7 million in installments through 2027. "We expect to fund the outlined payments from the ongoing sales of Yutrepia and cash on hand," Chief Financial Officer Michael Kaseta said. Liquidia has also asked the US Food and Drug Administration to remove PH-ILD from Yutrepia's label. Meanwhile, United Therapeutics said it has "established programs to help enable eligible patients to quickly and seamlessly transition to nebulized Tyvaso or Tyvaso DPI without interruption for their treatment." The settlement is largely favorable to both companies, according to analysts. "With the legal overhang removed, we now view Liquidia primarily as a Yutrepia growth story in PAH, with upside from label expansion plus significant pipeline opportunities from L606," Jefferies analyst Manoj Eradath said. L606 is Liquidia's experimental lung disease drug, currently in late-stage development. Although the outcome was on par with investor expectations, the roughly $380 million payment was "better than expected" for United Therapeutics, according to J.P. Morgan analyst Jessica Fye. It would also likely improve visibility into future Tyvaso growth in PH-ILD, said Jefferies analyst Roger Song. Shares of United Therapeutics were down nearly 1% in morning trading. Meanwhile, Liquidia will terminate trial cohorts studying PH-ILD and cease publication of related data as part of the settlement, according to a regulatory filing by United Therapeutics.

item.title: Trump tariff threat built a US copper mountain, but the effects are fading
item.description: President Donald Trump’s tariff threat helped to build copper stockpiles of more than 1 million metric tons in the United States without spending public money, but the flow is slowing as traders await a decision on the levies.
item.dc:creator: Pratima Desai
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump’s tariff threat helped to build copper stockpiles of more than 1 million metric tons in the United States without spending public money, but the flow is slowing as traders await a decision on the levies. The prospect of levies has left Comex-approved warehouses in the United States holding roughly 70% of the world's visible copper stocks. This has created shortages elsewhere, fuelling a price surge despite a global surplus. "Only traders are making money. There are cheaper ways they could have got the copper. They could have quietly collected metal around the world from the off-exchange market," said Panmure Liberum analyst Tom Price. Whether and when tariffs are imposed on US imports and whether the possibility will keep attracting copper will be a key talking point at LME Week, the industry's annual gathering in London, starting on October 18. Traders have been shipping copper to the United States since Trump ordered a study on the potential for tariffs in February last year, which pushed Comex prices to record highs, reaching $6.83 a lb, or $15,057 a ton, on September 22. This created a positive arbitrage — a price gap — in favour of Comex over London Metal Exchange copper , once costs including freight and insurance were stripped out. The arb hit a record peak above $3,000 a ton in July last year. Since then, it has been high enough to make shipping copper to the United States profitable, but not always. The arb is now about $310 a ton. "The US built a copper stockpile without spending taxpayer money, with policy and an almost existential threat of import levies," said Wood Mackenzie analyst Charles Cooper. "But the arbitrage has collapsed, so the incentive to keep moving metal to the US is much weaker right now." JANUARY DECISION DEADLINE LOOMS The US Commerce Department was due to report on the domestic copper market by June 30 so Trump could decide whether to impose a 15% tariff on refined copper imports from January 1, 2027, rising to 30% in 2028. But no decision has been announced. One scenario Macquarie analyst Alice Fox sees as most likely is that the January deadline passes without a decision, leaving the question of tariffs unresolved. "This would likely see the arb come off in the short term but then return to current levels ... not quite high enough to encourage additional metal, but high enough to keep metal in the US," Fox said. Macquarie estimates that copper stocks in the United States on and off exchange now total about 1.6 million tons. Since the end of February last year, Comex copper stocks have climbed nearly 750% to more than 714,000 tons. Copper stored in LME warehouses in New Orleans and Baltimore have jumped 44% since mid-August to nearly 130,000 tons. Comex, Shanghai Futures Exchange and LME copper stocks overall total more than 1 million tons. LARGE SURPLUS IN THE US The US now has vastly more copper than it needs, which Panmure Liberum's Price expects to amount to 1.6 million tons this year. Numbers from information provider Trade Data Monitor show that the US imported more than 1.62 million tons of copper last year, up 80% from 2024. US Geological Survey pegged US production at 1 million tons last year, which left the US with a surplus. Analysts expect a similar picture this year. For excess metal to be exported, prices on the LME and the Shanghai Futures Exchange would need to be significantly above those on Comex. This will happen only when shortages outside the United States become critical. "When traders see surpluses in the US and severe shortages elsewhere, copper prices in the US and on the LME will be priced accordingly," said Price.

item.title: Ukraine says SpaceX hampers drones for attack and defence, as US ties fray
item.description: Ukraine said Elon Musk's SpaceX had limited its satellite services on Wednesday, hampering Ukrainian drones for attack missions and air defences, as relations between Kyiv and Washington have taken a sharp turn for the worse.
item.dc:creator: Yuliia Dysa, Dan Peleschuk
item.content:encoded: Ukraine said Elon Musk's SpaceX had limited its satellite services on Wednesday, hampering Ukrainian drones for attack missions and air defences, as relations between Kyiv and Washington have taken a sharp turn for the worse. Russia rained more missiles and drones down on Ukrainian cities, knocking out electricity for hundreds of thousands of people in attacks President Volodymyr Zelenskiy called "ostentatious disrespect" to Donald Trump's call for an energy ceasefire. The US president publicly turned on Zelenskiy in recent days after abruptly lifting sanctions on Russian diesel last week, under political pressure to lower fuel prices that have soared since he launched a war against Iran. He has called on Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian refineries, and said Ukrainians should replace their wartime leader. "It's painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side," Zelenskiy told Piers Morgan Uncensored. He said that [USN:L8N46022D TEXT:"he was OK"] with Trump being in the middle of Ukraine and Russia, but added: "If you are in the middle, you have to stay in the middle." Asked about the restriction on the military version of SpaceX's Starlink services in Ukraine, Zelenskiy said: "It's a big mistake ... this decision will bring a lot of human losses." He did not say who was responsible. Trump announced at the weekend that Ukraine and Russia both agreed to halt attacks on energy targets, although neither side confirmed this and the past two days have seen intensive Russian bombing, including of Ukrainian power stations. After a night of bombardment of the capital Kyiv, Russian strikes continued throughout the day on Wednesday with six people killed in the western city of Lutsk, where the regional governor said a warehouse and a residential building were hit. Ukraine, for its part, continued long-range strikes on Russia, hitting [USN:L8N46009S TEXT:"Russia's biggest data centre"], although it says it is holding back from hitting energy targets for now to show respect for Trump. NO WARNING BEFORE STARLINK CUTS Ukrainian military officials said Musk's SpaceX (SPCX.O) had without warning started to interrupt functioning of its military-grade terminals when they are moving at high speed. Kyiv installs SpaceX receptors in many of its drones as part of their onboard guidance systems. The terminals operate across Ukraine, including in territory held by Russian forces. "Our defence forces did not receive a warning about this limitation, and this led to the disruption of several missions," presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram, saying the restriction affected StarShield, SpaceX's military and intelligence service. The speed cutoff hampers Ukraine's ability to conduct strikes on Russian targets inside Ukraine, or to defend itself from Russian drones using its own interceptor drones, according to a defence ministry source and another military source. Beskrestnov said SpaceX had imposed a speed limit of 160 km per hour. The defence ministry source told Reuters military units had reported guidance systems losing their connections at speeds of less than half that. SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The defence ministry source said Ukraine was in contact with the company as well as the US government and NATO to seek clarification over the sudden limitations. The suggestion that Musk's company had limited Ukrainian military capabilities drew a sharp response from Poland, which pays for Ukrainian Starlink subscriptions on Kyiv's behalf. "Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski asked Musk on X. "As your European customers, we are watching you." There was no immediate response from Musk, who in the past has called Sikorski a "small man". Shares in European satellite operator Eutelsat (ETL.PA) , which is seen as Europe's best shot at taking on Starlink, [USN:L6N4600QK TEXT:"jumped on Wednesday"] as some investors bet that European providers could benefit from growing strains between Washington and Kyiv. Musk is a close political ally of Trump, and the suggestion that SpaceX might limit Ukrainian capabilities reinforced wider Ukrainian concerns that Washington could withhold battlefield support to compel its one-time ally to make concessions. Sources have told Reuters and other media that the US has threatened to cut off intelligence for early warning of missile strikes on Ukraine, to press Kyiv to suspend attacks on Russian oil refineries. NO WARNING AHEAD OF MISSILES Rescue workers in Kyiv were stretchering the injured from the wreckage of a blasted-out residential building overnight, while firefighters battled a huge blaze in the darkness. Officials said 2 people were killed and 21 wounded at the site. Some 600,000 people were left without power as Russian missiles careened into power stations during hours of attacks that primarily targeted Kyiv and Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city. Russia's defence ministry confirmed it had struck four power plants in and around Kyiv and two in Kharkiv, among other targets. Zelenskiy said 30 energy facilities were damaged. Ukrainian officials said late on Tuesday they had received no warnings from Western partners for a second day before Russian missiles hit the capital. Trump had insisted on Tuesday that Washington was [USN:L1N45Z0GP TEXT:"still sharing intelligence"]. Zelenskiy cast the latest Russian attacks as a deliberate snub to Trump's declaration of a ceasefire on energy targets. "Russia does not consider the American President's statements strong," Zelenskiy wrote on X. "The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States." Zelenskiy has said Ukraine is willing to observe an energy ceasefire and has not targeted Russian refineries since Trump announced it, but will not continue to hold back if Russia ignores the purported truce. The Kremlin said on Tuesday that contacts were continuing about an energy truce. Ukraine reported downing just 4 out of 39 Russian missiles, reflecting Kyiv's weakened air defences against fast-moving ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones amid a shortage of weapons.

item.title: US bank regulator faults several large lenders over debanking practices
item.description: A top US bank regulator issued a report on Wednesday finding some of the country's largest banks unfairly denied services to some clients on political, religious or other grounds, but stopped short of imposing penalties.
item.dc:creator: Pete Schroeder, Manya Saini
item.content:encoded: A top US bank regulator issued a report on Wednesday finding some of the country's largest banks unfairly denied services to some clients on political, religious or other grounds, but stopped short of imposing penalties. The [USN:L4N4491DY TEXT:"debanking"] report from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency covered nine of the nation's largest banks by asset size. The regulator found each had policies restricting some clients' access to financial services based on subjective criteria rather than financial risk. Banks have said they close accounts or deny services because of legal, financial or reputational risks, not politics. The regulator criticized the banks for the practices, but did not indicate any sanctions or punishments were forthcoming. It said it may consider policy changes to discourage such activity. FAIR ACCESS IS A MANDATE: REGULATOR The review, which began in September 2025, scrutinized banks that collectively hold a majority of US commercial banking assets. "Americans should have access to financial services regardless of their beliefs, affiliations, or political views. Fair access to financial services is not a mantra — it is a mandate," Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould said in a statement. After President Donald Trump signed an executive order directing a review of alleged debanking, [USN:L4N42C182 TEXT:"regulators and banks moved to eliminate the use of reputation risk "]in assessing clients, though[USN:L4N4491DY TEXT:" the issue remains contentious. "] Conservative politicians and business groups have accused banks of cutting off companies in sectors including fossil fuels, firearms and cryptocurrency , making debanking a flashpoint in Washington financial policy. Large banks have denied rejecting customers on political or religious grounds, arguing instead that years of aggressive regulatory pressure discouraged them from serving certain sectors and urging Washington to establish clearer rules on who they can and cannot serve. The OCC found that concerns about public opinion had led at least one bank to distance itself from certain customer affiliations that could be viewed as partisan. It added that banks generally lacked clear, measurable standards and objective, risk-based criteria for assessing reputational risks associated with customer relationships. "The OCC will continue to work with our regulatory partners to further assess the extent to which bank policies implementing money laundering and terrorist financing program requirements have contributed to debanking and will take appropriate action as needed," the report said. Earlier this year, Trump [USN:L4N3YN1QS TEXT:"filed a $5 billion lawsuit"] against JPMorgan Chase and its CEO Jamie Dimon, alleging the bank closed several of his accounts for political reasons. JPMorgan, the largest US bank, has denied closing accounts on political or religious grounds, and filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit on Tuesday. A bank spokesperson said the lender prohibits political and religious discrimination, and added, "Years of operating in a regulatory environment that often second-guessed decisions contributed to a culture of caution across the banking industry. That system needs fixing." Trump has also [USN:S0N3OG012 TEXT:"accused other lenders"], including Bank of America (BAC.N) , the country's second-biggest lender by assets, of debanking him in early 2025. A Bank of America spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the new report. The bank has previously said it does not comment on client matters and would welcome clearer rules from bank regulators on how to conduct its activities.

item.title: Eutelsat shares jump as Ukraine flags curbs on Starlink military-grade service
item.description: Shares in European satellite operator Eutelsat soared on Wednesday after Ukraine said SpaceX's Starlink had introduced restrictions on its military-grade service, fuelling investor bets that European providers could benefit from growing strains between Washington and Kyiv.
item.dc:creator: Gianluca Lo Nostro, Hugo Lhomedet
item.content:encoded: Shares in European satellite operator Eutelsat (ETL.PA) soared on Wednesday after Ukraine said SpaceX's (SPCX.O) Starlink [USN:L1N46007X TEXT:"had introduced restrictions"] on its military-grade service, fuelling investor bets that European providers could benefit from growing strains between Washington and Kyiv. Eutelsat, which is seen as Europe's best shot at taking on Starlink, surged 23% by 1355 GMT, the stock's biggest one-day gain in 16 months. Luxembourg-based rival SES , which also provides satellite connectivity services, rose 2.6%. Analysts said the move reflected investor expectations that European governments and customers could seek alternatives to US-owned space assets if access to American services becomes less certain. "I think this is related to the US administration's favourable Russia/unfavourable Ukraine stance that has developed in recent days, meaning no or limited access to US-owned satellite services and intelligence sharing, putting European providers back in the spotlight as potential alternatives," Bernstein analyst Aleksander Peterc said. Eutelsat is currently the only other company in the world besides SpaceX that provides space-based internet services through its OneWeb network of satellites in low Earth orbit. But Starlink, which targets consumers directly, has around 10,000 satellites in orbit compared with Eutelsat's more than 600. Investors appear to be betting that geopolitical tensions could drive demand towards European satellite operators. Experts caution, however, that existing Starlink users cannot simply migrate to OneWeb and that any transition would require the deployment of new terminals and supporting infrastructure. "OneWeb may provide useful complementary capacity, but considering it as a straightforward substitute overlooks significant operational and infrastructure constraints," independent satellite consultant Christian Freiherr von der Ropp said. Replacing Starlink or Starshield would require the deployment of large numbers of new user terminals, he said, while adding OneWeb's smaller constellation and different network architecture could limit its usefulness in some military applications.

item.title: Crudo sube por ataques en Arabia Saudita y nuevas tácticas de Irán para atacar tanqueros
item.description: El petróleo subía el miércoles, tras un ataque de los hutíes contra Saudi Aramco y luego de que Irán anunciara que está aplicando nuevas tácticas para atacar buques con el objetivo de mantener altos los precios.
item.dc:creator: Nicole Jao
item.content:encoded: El petróleo subía el miércoles, tras un ataque de los hutíes contra Saudi Aramco y luego de que Irán anunciara que está aplicando nuevas tácticas para atacar buques con el objetivo de mantener altos los precios. * A las 1725 GMT, los futuros del Brent subían 87 centavos, o un 0,82%, a 106,56 dólares el barril, y los del West Texas Intermediate en Estados Unidos (WTI) ganaban 1,46 dólares, o un 1,55%, a 95,60 dólares, tocando un pico de tres semanas. * "Los ataques a buques que cruzan el estrecho de Ormuz y los ataques militares entre Arabia Saudita y los hutíes están respaldando los precios, ya que los actores del mercado siguen preocupados por la disminución de las exportaciones petroleras en la región", afirmó Giovanni Staunovo, analista de UBS. * Las autoridades iraníes se negaron a dar detalles sobre la nueva estrategia para atacar a los buques, pero una de ellas afirmó que Teherán había comenzado a emplear diferentes tácticas ofensivas hace unos 10 días. * "El hecho de que las autoridades iraníes admitan abiertamente que están socavando los esfuerzos de Estados Unidos por mantener los precios del petróleo bajo control dice mucho de las verdaderas intenciones que se esconden tras las llamadas 'conversaciones de paz'", señaló Priyanka Sachdeva, de Phillip Nova. Los flujos de petróleo del Golfo, excluido Irán, se dispararon en septiembre hasta superar el 81% de los niveles previos a la guerra, según datos, impulsados por la recuperación de las exportaciones sauditas. Las exportaciones iraníes cayeron a cero debido al bloqueo estadounidense. "Que llegue más crudo a los mercados internacionales no significa necesariamente que se esté produciendo más petróleo", señaló en una nota Ole Hansen, analista de Saxo Bank. "Parte de la recuperación refleja una redistribución de los barriles disponibles, incluidos los volúmenes que, de otro modo, habrían abastecido a las refinerías regionales". * Los hutíes atacaron un edificio administrativo perteneciente a la petrolera estatal Saudi Aramco (2222.SE) en la ciudad de Dhahran, lo que provocó un incendio de alcance limitado, informó el miércoles el Ministerio de Energía saudí. * El grupo ha lanzado misiles balísticos y drones contra Arabia Saudita durante la última semana en represalia por el apoyo del reino a las fuerzas gubernamentales yemeníes. El aeropuerto internacional de Riad ha sido alcanzado en cuatro ocasiones, y un ataque perpetrado el sábado causó la muerte de 13 personas. * Por otra parte, un buque portacontenedores se hundió en el sur del estrecho de Ormuz tras chocar contra una mina naval y prenderse fuego, informó la Marina de la Guardia Revolucionaria de Irán. * Un día antes, el Centro de Operaciones de Comercio Marítimo de Reino Unido informó que un portacontenedores y un petrolero habían sido alcanzados por proyectiles de origen desconocido en el estrecho.

item.title: BofA misses profit estimates on trading weakness, books $1.2 billion charge
item.description: Bank of America missed third-quarter profit estimates on Wednesday due to weakness in its trading business and disclosed a $1.2 billion charge tied to a regulatory penalty over failures to detect potential money-laundering activity.
item.dc:creator: Arasu Basil, Saeed Azhar
item.content:encoded: Bank of America (BAC.N) missed third-quarter profit estimates on Wednesday due to weakness in its trading business and disclosed a $1.2 billion charge tied to a regulatory penalty over failures to detect potential money-laundering activity. Shares of the second-biggest US lender fell more than 8%, hitting their lowest price since May. The Wall Street giant posted weaker fixed income, currency and commodities revenue, mirroring third-quarter trends at rivals [USN:L4N45Z10B TEXT:"JPMorgan Chase"] (JPM.N) , [USN:L4N45Z0VX TEXT:"Wells Fargo"] (WFC.N) and [USN:L4N45Z111 TEXT:"Goldman Sachs"] (GS.N) . "The poor capital markets performance doubles the negative impact of the earnings miss," Zacks Investment Management Chief Market Strategist Brian Mulberry said. BofA's sales and trading revenue fell 5% to $5.1 billion in the quarter, as weakness in FICC overshadowed record quarterly equities trading. The bank had last month projected quarterly sales and trading revenue to be relatively flat compared to last year. Bank of America also showed unrealized losses on its bond portfolio - mortgage backed securities and U.S. Treasury, government-agency bonds - at $109 billion in the quarter ended September, up from $85 billion at the end of June, as bond yields rose in the last quarter. Bulk of these securities were in held-to-maturity segment, which the bank does not intend to sell. Banks use the held-to-maturity designation to buy less risky securities that give them downside protection, even though in a rising interest rate environment there is limited upside potential. "Reduced client activity and changing market conditions, including a major shift in interest rates, significantly affected our leading FICC businesses, including credit mortgages and municipals," Chief Financial Officer Alastair Borthwick said. Rival JPMorgan on Tuesday also [USN:L4N45Z10B TEXT:"fell short"] of quarterly profit estimates as dealmaking, bond trading momentum slowed down. Asked how much longer he plans on remaining BofA's CEO, Brian Moynihan said succession is the board's decision. Moynihan has been at the helm of the storied US bank since 2010 and is one of the longest-serving CEOs of a major US bank. REGULATORY SETTLEMENT CHARGE The fine, [USN:L6N45Z18I TEXT:"unveiled late Tuesday"], stems from BofA's failure to report over $5 billion in suspicious activity to the US government. The actions, which include the third-largest penalty in US Treasury history, highlight [USN:L6N45U1B5 TEXT:"growing regulatory scrutiny"] of shortcomings in tackling money laundering at US financial giants. "There's no asset cap here. It won't crowd out anything," Borthwick told analysts. Regulators have placed BofA under a consent order — a major regulatory punishment — that requires the bank to work with a third party to identify and report suspicious transactions that went undetected. BofA had been working with regulators for some time to reach the resolutions, Borthwick said, adding the bank had added thousands of people to shore up its efforts to tackle money laundering. The Charlotte, North Carolina-based bank reported a profit of $6.9 billion, or 91 cents per share, for the three months ended September 30, compared with $8.3 billion, or $1.04 per share, a year earlier. Excluding the $1.2 billion regulatory settlement charge, BofA earned $1.08 per share, missing estimates of $1.10 per share, according to estimates compiled by LSEG. Wall Street analysts said the penalty would likely add to negative sentiment and raise concerns about expenses and the duration of the order. The penalty follows a 2024 consent order from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, which had required BofA to address shortcomings in its ability to police money laundering. Since late 2023, BofA has been working with US regulators to overhaul its safeguards against money laundering and other illegal transactions. NII SHINES AS DEALMAKING WEAKENS BofA's investment banking fees fell 11% to $1.8 billion in the quarter. The bank had last month projected a decline of at least 10%, as it wasn't well positioned in some businesses that saw more activity. Dealmaking also slowed in the reported quarter as a grinding bond market rout and equities volatility weighed on activity. "There's a period in volatility like that where buyers and sellers just need to readjust valuations and expectations. So that always happens," Borthwick said, referring to the move in interest rates. Investment banking fees can be lumpy from quarter-to-quarter and are influenced by when deals close. Transaction timing can often move around due to market conditions and regulatory approvals. "The environment for deal making remains solid. It's a pretty active environment," Borthwick said, adding that BofA's investment banking pipelines are strong. BofA slipped to fourth place in the global investment banking league table for the first nine months of 2026, from third in the same period a year earlier, Dealogic data showed. In a bright spot, net interest income (NII) — the difference between what a bank earns on loans and pays out on deposits — jumped 8% in the quarter, driven by higher loan and deposit balances and fixed-rate asset repricing. BofA expects interest income to improve sequentially in the fourth-quarter. Full-year NII growth is anticipated to be 8% or more in 2027.

item.title: Oro baja más de 1% por mayores apuestas de alza tasas Fed tras datos inflación EEUU
item.description: El oro bajó más de un 1% el miércoles, sumando su tercera ronda de descensos seguida, ya que unos datos de inflación superiores a lo esperado aumentaron las expectativas de que la Reserva Federal suba las tasas de interés este mes.
item.dc:creator: Vishak Mathew
item.content:encoded: El oro bajó más de un 1% el miércoles, sumando su tercera ronda de descensos seguida, ya que unos datos de inflación superiores a lo esperado aumentaron las expectativas de que la Reserva Federal suba las tasas de interés este mes. * A las 1805 GMT, el oro al contado cedía un 1,8% a 4.083,94 dólares por onza, su menor nivel desde el 7 de octubre, mientras que los futuros del oro en Estados Unidos para entrega en diciembre bajaron un 1,7% a 4.107,90 dólares. * El índice dólar (.DXY) subía un 0,5%, encareciendo el oro denominado en esa moneda para los tenedores de otras divisas, mientras que los rendimientos de los bonos del Tesoro a 10 años también aumentaron. * "En este momento, todo apunta a que es más probable que la Fed suba las tasas", afirmó David Meger, director de operaciones con metales de High Ridge Futures, citando los datos del índice de precios al consumo (IPC), más altos de lo esperado, que se han mantenido por encima de los objetivos de la Fed. * Los precios al consumidor en Estados Unidos se aceleraron en septiembre por un repunte en los precios de la gasolina, en un nuevo revés para el presidente Donald Trump y su Partido Republicano antes de las elecciones legislativas de noviembre. * El IPC subió un 0,6% el mes pasado, tras registrar un aumento del 0,4% en agosto, informó la Oficina de Estadísticas Laborales del Departamento de Trabajo. * Los mercados estiman que hay un 42% de probabilidades de que la Fed suba las tasas este mes, frente al 22% antes de conocerse los datos de inflación, y descuentan una probabilidad del 93% de que se produzca un alza en diciembre, según la herramienta FedWatch de CME. * Aunque el oro suele considerarse una cobertura contra la inflación, el aumento de las tasas de interés tiende a reducir el atractivo de este metal precioso, que no devenga intereses. * El petróleo subía el miércoles, tras un ataque de los hutíes contra Saudi Aramco y luego de que Irán anunciara que está aplicando nuevas tácticas para atacar buques con el objetivo de mantener altos los precios. * En otros metales preciosos, la plata al contado perdía un 6,6% a 55,53 dólares por onza; el platino restaba un 3,5%, a 1.605,37 dólares; y el paladio cedía un 2,8% a 1.094,50 dólares.

item.title: Ohio's working-class voters rethink support for Trump and the Republican Party
item.description: A decade after Republican Donald Trump peeled away working-class and union voters who had long been a cornerstone of Democratic support in Ohio, Democrats and labor leaders see an opening to win back some of them in the November 3 US elections.
item.dc:creator: Richard Cowan
item.content:encoded: A decade after Republican Donald Trump peeled away working-class and union voters who had long been a cornerstone of Democratic support in Ohio, Democrats and labor leaders see an opening to win back some of them in the November 3 US elections . Now midway through his second term, the president's magic appears to be losing at least some of its luster with blue-collar men and women as rising prices, the Iran war and concerns about his rhetoric prompt some voters to reconsider their support. The state's reputation as a leading swing state began to fade in 2016 when Trump won strong support from working-class voters who felt their economic concerns were being heard, helping turn Ohio into a reliably Republican state. Almost overnight, Ohio became rock-solid Republican. Ohio voted for the eventual winner in 14 straight presidential elections from 1964 until 2020 when Democrat Joe Biden won nationally but Ohio backed Trump. A shift in Ohio toward Democrats could matter in elections that will help determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress during Trump's final two years in office or hand new leverage [USN:L6N45U0XV TEXT:"to Democrats"] over his agenda. The stakes are high in Ohio, where Republicans are defending a US Senate seat and the governor's office. Two House races are rated [USN:L1N45R0LS TEXT:""toss-ups.""] One, in northwestern Ohio, has long been held by a Democrat and the other, in northeastern Ohio, is Republican-held. Trump is not on the ballot this time but has told supporters to act as if he is. It remains to be seen whether that could end up helping or hindering Republicans running in tough races. Republican Senator Jon Husted is in a tight competition with Democratic former Senator Sherrod Brown, while Democrat Amy Acton is challenging Republican Vivek Ramaswamy for an open governor's seat. Trump campaigned with Husted and Ramaswamy in Youngstown on Monday to try to energize the Republican base. 'GOD KNOWS WE DIDN'T VOTE FOR THIS' Paul Ringold, a 48-year-old steel hauler and pastor of the mostly Black congregation at the Shalom Church of God and Christ in the city of Warren, embodies the uncertainty that Democrats hope could help them make inroads with working-class voters. Ringold voted for Trump for president in 2016, Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 and Trump again in 2024, but said he remains undecided about whom to support for the US Senate, governor and other offices this year. "I'm in the wilderness trying to find a place," he said. Ringold said rising fuel and food prices and Trump's combative style have left him questioning some of the choices made by a president he once strongly supported. "God knows we didn't vote for this," he said of inflation. Like several voters interviewed by Reuters, Ringold also cited Trump's rhetoric. "I wish he would just tone down that rhetoric ... that old New York in-your-face 'I got you sucker'" persona, he said. EARLY TURNOUT FAVORS DEMOCRATS In early voting that began in Ohio last week, Democrats appeared to be more motivated than Republicans. In Trumbull County, home to the city of Warren and many blue-collar jobs, a strong turnout during the first three days brought 1,224 Democrats to the polls, 559 Republicans and 453 with no known political affiliation, according to county data. Paul Sracic, an Ohio-based senior fellow with the right-of-center Hudson Institute, said "working-class voters, if they are moving at all away from Trump, Brown is a safe landing spot for them" because of the former senator's populist record. "Trump has done a good job of basically focusing on social issues with our guys," said Jose Arroyo, a United Steelworkers official who engages in contract negotiations and labor relations for the sprawling labor union. Trump "seemed to latch on sort of to the dissatisfaction of where the working man has gone. Pensions go away. Plants close. Livelihoods they've always known disappear." The problem, he said, is that focusing primarily on hot-button social issues ignores advancing policies that would "improve the lives of working people" and actually turn them into law. The 50,000 manufacturing jobs in 1990 in the Youngstown-Warren area fell to about 20,000 in 2026, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics. In recent years, the Mahoning Valley, long a powerhouse of the steel and automotive industries, has attracted a few new manufacturing plants. Arroyo said the Iran war has boosted domestic oil industry exploration, creating more demand for equipment made of steel. But he acknowledged that the war had also brought higher consumer prices. NLRB 'DISMANTLING' When Trump began his second term in January 2025, he promptly [USN:L2N3OO0LL TEXT:"fired"] two Democratic officials at the National Labor Relations Board and left the agency without the quorum required to take actions. That paralysis lasted [USN:L1N3XM0FP TEXT:"for nearly a year."] Ohio AFL-CIO President Tim Burga cited what he called Trump's "dismantling" of the NLRB as having hindered union organizing efforts and made it harder to contest unfair labor practices and secure work contracts with companies. "We were on a path for the first time in my lifetime, under the Biden administration, for having a national industrial policy," Burga said, but the Trump administration rolled much of it back. [USN:L2N3S70NN TEXT:"Biden and Congress enacted programs"] to spur investment in such industries as clean energy and semiconductors. Trump's trade battles with Canada also were unhelpful to labor, he said. OHIO VOTERS REMAIN DIVIDED Bill Callahan, 75, a self-described Democrat from Cortland, said some relatives who once backed Trump "are traveling back" toward Democrats because "they don't like (politicians) taking money out of their pockets." A part-time warehouse worker from Cortland after a career at General Electric, he said he considered voting for Trump in 2016 but was put off by ethical concerns. Others interviewed by Reuters said higher prices were not enough to change their vote. Joe Scarabino, who co-owns a bait-and-tackle business with his wife Kathryn near Cortland, said the couple responded to higher fuel costs by raising delivery charges rather than product prices, thus having an impact on fewer customers and small business owners. "We believe our Christian values are more than gas prices," he said. The couple declined to say who they support. Retired coal-fired power plant worker Chuck Burns, 67, of Wellsville, credited Trump with reducing illegal immigration and boosting the value of his retirement investments. "He's done a good job ... he's got balls," Burns said. Burns praised Trump's immigration restrictions at the southern border and said his retirement savings have increased in value since Biden left office. Asked what issues worry him in this election season, Burns said, "It's just that Democrats – it's unbelievable some of the stuff that they want to do." Asked to explain, Burns raised transgender issues. "Those poor people, they feel that way, that's fine, that's their business," he said. "They (Democrats) don't need to incorporate our young kids into that stuff."

item.title: Wall Street tumbles as hot inflation data feeds worries about Fed rate hikes
item.description: Hotter-than-expected inflation data sent Wall Street tumbling on Wednesday, with worries about more interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve pummeling shares of Oracle, CoreWeave and other AI stocks sensitive to higher borrowing costs.
item.dc:creator: Noel Randewich, Purvi Agarwal
item.content:encoded: Hotter-than-expected inflation data sent Wall Street tumbling on Wednesday, with worries about more interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve pummeling shares of Oracle, CoreWeave and other AI stocks sensitive to higher borrowing costs. Increased bets that the Fed will have to further hike rates to tame inflation dealt a [USN:L4N4601KQ TEXT:"sharp blow"] to some of the market's biggest gainers of 2026. Oracle (ORCL.N) lost 7.3%, while AI-infrastructure firms CoreWeave (CRWV.O) and Nebius (NBIS.O) tumbled 15% and 10%, respectively. Dell (DELL.N) dropped 12% and Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE.N) lost 7.6% after Barclays downgraded the AI server makers to "equal-weight" from "overweight".
