The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index (.SOX) dropped almost 4%, down for a sixth straight session and on track for its longest losing streak since May 2025. US consumer prices [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"accelerated"] in September as the cost of gasoline surged and price pressures broadened beyond energy, data from the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics showed. Interest rate traders are pricing in a 37% chance that the Fed will raise rates at its policy meeting this month, up from 22% on Tuesday, according to CME's FedWatch tool. "Investors are not happy with the report because that puts pressure on the Fed to raise rates to combat inflation," said Adam Sarhan, chief executive of 50 Park Investments, in New York. "Inflation remains public enemy number one for the market and for the Fed." The S&P 500 was down 1.35% at 7,700.08 points. The Nasdaq declined 2.02% to 26,654.96 points, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 0.51% at 51,405.02 points. Eight of the 11 S&P 500 sector indexes declined, led lower by information technology (.SPLRCT) , down 2.64%, followed by a 1.77% loss in communication services (.SPLRCL) . After hitting a record high last week, the S&P 500 remains up over 12% in 2026, with most of that gain fueled by AI-related stocks. The median S&P 500 stock has gained 4% in 2026, and over 200 of the index's components are in negative territory. Bank of America (BAC.N) fell 5.8%. The lender's [USN:L4N4600WF TEXT:"profit fell"] in the third quarter as it set aside $1.2 billion to cover regulatory fines for failures to detect potential money laundering. Morgan Stanley (MS.N) dropped 3.8%, despite a [USN:L4N4600Y8 TEXT:"rise in quarterly profit"]. The S&P 500 Banks index (.SPXBK) was last down 1.2%. Earlier, it dipped more than 2% to its lowest level in over four months. Asset manager BlackRock (BLK.N) was near flat after reporting a jump in[USN:L4N4600US TEXT:" third-quarter profit"]. The Fed has time to wait and see how markets and the economy evolve after its September rate rise before deciding further action, Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said. Bending Spoons (BSP.O) rallied 45% after Berkshire Hathaway (BRKa.N) invested another [USN:L4N4601HL TEXT:"$330 million"] in the owner of Vimeo and AOL, a big endorsement from the high-profile investor whose moves traders closely follow. Declining stocks outnumbered rising ones within the S&P 500 (.AD.SPX) by a 1.7-to-one ratio. The S&P 500 posted 14 new highs and 11 new lows; the Nasdaq recorded 22 new highs and 466 new lows.

item.title: BHP, Escondida supervisors reach deal to avert strike at Chile copper mine
item.description: BHP and the supervisors' union at its Escondida mine in Chile have struck a deal over improved compensation and benefits, avoiding a strike at the world's largest copper mine, both parties said on Wednesday.
item.dc:creator: Fabian Cambero
item.content:encoded: BHP (BHP.AX) and the supervisors' union at its Escondida mine in Chile have struck a deal over improved compensation and benefits, avoiding a strike at the world's largest copper mine, both parties said on Wednesday. The threat of a stoppage at Escondida had helped support copper prices and, along with low LME copper inventories, fuelled supply concerns for the metal widely used in the power, construction and manufacturing sectors. The union said in a statement announcing the deal that 64% of its members had accepted the company's proposal while 35% refused. "The offer presented today is approved by the union, thus concluding the 2026 regulated collective bargaining process," it added. BHP said that the new contract is valid for 36 months and includes improvements in fixed and variable compensation and current benefits, also incorporating new bonuses and other benefits. Two sources familiar with the talks had earlier [USN:L6N4600KA TEXT:"told Reuters"] that negotiators struck a tentative deal after the company improved its offer. "The parties reached a pre-agreement that includes improved benefits and better closing terms than the offer presented by the company on October 12," the union had said in an earlier statement. BHP's previous offer included final payments and a low-interest loan package worth about $30,000 per worker. The talks began [USN:L6N45Z1D0 TEXT:"hours earlier on Tuesday"] in a last-minute push to avoid a walkout that risked disrupting supply from a mine central to the global copper market. The union had warned it was prepared to strike as early as Wednesday if mediation failed to produce a new collective labor agreement.

item.title: Supervisores de mina chilena Escondida de BHP evitan huelga y aceptan nuevo contrato
item.description: Los supervisores de la mina chilena Escondida, controlada por BHP, aprobaron el miércoles un nuevo contrato colectivo de 36 meses, lo que evitó una huelga en el mayor yacimiento global de cobre.
item.dc:creator: Fabián Andrés Cambero
item.content:encoded: Los supervisores de la mina chilena Escondida, controlada por BHP, aprobaron el miércoles un nuevo contrato colectivo de 36 meses, lo que evitó una huelga en el mayor yacimiento global de cobre. Dos fuentes con conocimiento de las negociaciones informaron a Reuters en la madrugada del preacuerdo entre el gremio y la empresa, y que la propuesta ya redactada se presentaría a los socios del gremio para su ratificación. Tras el conteo, la propuesta tuvo una aprobación del 64,14% de los votos válidos frente a un rechazo del 35,85%. "La oferta presentada el día de hoy se entiende por aprobada por la base sindical y con esto ha finalizado el proceso de negociación colectiva reglada", dijo el sindicato en un boletín a sus socios. La noche del martes el sindicato había anunciado [USN:L6N45Z1D4 TEXT:"un fracaso de las negociaciones y el inicio de la paralización"] en el primer turno del miércoles, pero después fueron citados nuevamente por el mediador a una nueva reunión que se extendió durante toda la noche y culminó con la redacción del nuevo instrumento colectivo. El gremio detalló en un comunicado más temprano que se realizaría la votación online para avalar el resultado obtenido. BHP confirmó que las partes ya firmaron el acuerdo, con lo que quedó cerrada la negociación. "El nuevo contrato tiene una vigencia de 36 meses y contiene mejoras significativas en compensaciones fijas, variables y beneficios actuales, incorporando además nuevos bonos y otros beneficios. De esta manera, los Supervisores y Staff siguen contando con un contrato líder en la industria para el segmento", dijo la empresa en un comunicado. Previamente, BHP había informado que Escondida continuaba operando con normalidad. El temor de un huelga en Escondida y la paralización desde la semana pasada de la mina Centinela de Antofagasta Minerals han dado soporte a los precios globales del cobre en momentos en que la industria atraviesa dificultades para impulsar la oferta. La propuesta contempla pagos finales y préstamo blando por unos 30.500 dólares por socio. Escondida, enclavada en el norteño desierto de Atacama, es operada por BHP, pero está asociada con la global Rio Tinto y la japonesa JECO.

item.title: Stripchat loses legal fight against EU tech label
item.description: Adult content platform Stripchat, a subsidiary of Cyprus's Technius, on Thursday lost its legal challenge against EU tech regulators' decision to include it in a list of companies subject to stringent requirements under landmark online content rules after Europe's second-highest court rejected its arguments, a court statement said.
item.dc:creator: Yun Chee Foo
item.content:encoded: Adult content platform Stripchat, a subsidiary of Cyprus's Technius, on Thursday lost its legal challenge against EU tech regulators' decision to include it in a list of companies subject to stringent requirements under landmark online content rules after Europe's second-highest court rejected its arguments, a court statement said. Three years ago, the European Commission designated Stripchat and two other adult content companies as very large online platforms under the Digital Services Act which requires such companies to do more to tackle illegal and harmful content on their platforms. DSA breaches can cost companies fines as much as 6% of their global turnover. Stripchat subsequently sued the Commission, which is the EU tech enforcer, at the Luxembourg-based General Court. It disagreed with how the Commission calculated its number of users, a benchmark used to assess whether a company falls under the DSA. A court statement stated that the European Commission had given Stripchat adequate reasons for its decision. The ruling can be appealed on matters of law at the EU Court of Justice, Europe's top court. The case is T-134/24 Technius v Commission.

item.title: LSEG taps Nvidia for faster historical market data processing
item.description: The London Stock Exchange Group said on Wednesday it has partnered with Nvidia to help financial institutions process and analyse large volumes of historical market data faster and at scale using the US chipmaker's technology.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The London Stock Exchange Group (LSEG.L) said on Wednesday it has partnered with Nvidia (NVDA.O) to help financial institutions process and analyse large volumes of historical market data faster and at scale using the US chipmaker's technology. LSEG, which operates the London Stock Exchange and provides data and analytics, has been expanding its offerings to support diverse demand whilst retaining licenses and control as AI also affects how businesses trade and consume data. Analysis showed that computing on Nvidia's specialised processors without creating copies of the dataset could help study every trade and price quote in seconds for insights, the company said. This would make research faster and closer to real-time as equity trading moves to 24-hour cycles, it added. "This collaboration expands how customers can draw insight from LSEG's trusted, governed Tick History. Customers want to work with detailed historical data at speed," said Ron Lefferts, co-head of data & analytics at LSEG. According to the company, its Tick History has about 110 trillion rows of data across 100 million instruments spanning 30 years and 580 exchanges, trading venues and contributors. LSEG is the largest customer of Reuters, which provides news for its Workspace news and data platform and other products. It plans next year to launch [USN:L6N43M13O TEXT:"LSE 24"], a night-time trading site for some exchange-traded products.

item.title: Denmark says US resource exploration in Greenland must respect local laws
item.description: Denmark's foreign ministry said on Wednesday if the US wished to explore Greenland's resources, it would have to do so within the framework of the Arctic island's legislation, adding that last month's deal between the three parties did not change this.
item.dc:creator: Louise Rasmussen
item.content:encoded: Denmark's foreign ministry said on Wednesday if the US wished to explore Greenland's resources, it would have to do so within the framework of the Arctic island's legislation, adding that last month's deal between the three parties did not change this. US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that "massive oil, gas and mineral exploration" was set to begin on Greenland, a contentious statement on a territory that has resisted his efforts to control it and has banned new drilling for crude. Trump described the Danish Arctic island, which is run by a semi-autonomous government, as "our new and beautiful Greenland" in a social media post that hailed what he said were US gains from [USN:L6N45E07X TEXT:"a security deal"] signed in September. The Danish foreign ministry said in a statement that "the agreement does not grant investors from the US any preferential treatment compared with investors from other NATO countries, EU countries and NATO partners when it comes to access to natural resources in Greenland." The Greenlandic prime minister's office declined to comment on Trump's statement, while Greenland's ministry of mineral resources did not immediately respond to requests for comment. TRUMP HAILS US SECURITY GAINS Greenland has been caught up in [USN:L1N45D06G TEXT:"a confrontation"] with Trump, who has been saying since 2019 the US should buy or take the strategically located and [USN:L1N3YF0UH TEXT:"mineral-rich island"] for security reasons. On several occasions, he refused to rule out force. Along with Denmark, the US and Greenland reached an agreement last month to allow the US to boost its military presence on the island — a deal that had appeared to settle the standoff. The agreement did not allocate any rights for mining or drilling. "Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin," Trump wrote in a post on his Truth Social platform. "There are Experts that are saying that the amount of easily available Oil is far greater than that of almost any land, anywhere in the World," he added without naming any specific deals or specific development. Greenland banned uranium mining in its territory along with all future exploration of oil in 2021. The government has said it is reviewing whether a Texas firm, Greenland Energy (GLND.O) , can use permits predating that prohibition. The company said in August that it [USN:L6N45F0P1 TEXT:"had plans to drill"] for oil in 2027 at an untested basin on Greenland's east coast, although it lacked its own permit to do so. The previous owner, ARCO, spent heavily on seismic work in the 1970s but never drilled. Independent Danish security policy adviser Jacob Kaarsbo said Trump's comments could be seen as a sign that his desire to control Greenland remained unchanged. "It is extremely dangerous to view this agreement between the Trump administration and Denmark as something that has altered Trump's intentions," he said. The 10-page deal between the US, Denmark and Greenland paved the way for two new military bases and Trump's "Golden Dome" missile defence system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination. "Any future attack on the United States will have to come across Greenland, where our Defense will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet even conceived," Trump said in his post on Wednesday. "It gives us time, location, and sightline, like nowhere else in the World!" he added.

item.title: US to drop South Korea intelligence case against ex-CIA analyst
item.description: The US Justice Department has agreed to forgo prosecution of a former CIA analyst and White House National Security Council official who was accused of working as an unregistered agent for South Korea in exchange for luxury goods and other gifts.
item.dc:creator: Steve Gorman
item.content:encoded: The US Justice Department has agreed to forgo prosecution of a former CIA analyst and White House National Security Council official who was accused of working as an unregistered agent for South Korea in exchange for luxury goods and other gifts. Under a deferred prosecution deal reached with foreign policy specialist Sue Mi Terry, the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York said it would suspend criminal charges in the [USN:L1N3J80YP TEXT:"grand jury indictment"] returned against her in July 2024. Provided that Terry abides by several conditions stipulated in the deal, including restrictions on her travel and contacts with the government of South Korea, the case against her would be dropped altogether after 12 months of compliance. Terms of the agreement were laid out in a four-page deferred prosecution notice filed in US District Court in Manhattan on Tuesday. It gave Terry no explanation for why the Justice Department was essentially giving up its high-profile intelligence case except to say it had determined "that the interests of the United States and your own interest will be best served by deferring prosecution." The indictment accused Terry of accepting gifts from South Korea's government in return for advocating Seoul's policy positions, disclosing non-public information to its intelligence officers and facilitating access for South Korean government officials to their US counterparts. Her alleged work on behalf of South Korea as an unregistered foreign agent began in 2013, two years after she left US government employment, and ran for 10 years, including her time as a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations think tank. At the council, which placed her on unpaid leave following the indictment, she had worked as an expert on East Asia and Korean Peninsula. The indictment charged Terry with failing to register under the Foreign Agents Registration Act, and conspiring to violate that law. Terry has maintained her innocence. Her lawyer, Lee Wolosky, said at the time that his client had been a harsh critic of the Seoul government and that she was being prosecuted for performing the work of an independent scholar and news analyst. The unexpected outcome spares Terry the immediate threat of a criminal conviction or any jail time. It comes weeks before the case was set to go to trial, according to the New York Times. "We have consistently maintained that her interactions with South Korean officials were conducted in furtherance of US interests and her work as a leading American specialist on North Korea and East Asia," the Times quoted Wolosky as saying in a statement about the agreement. As part of the deal, Terry admitted to no wrongdoing. But she acknowledged assisting South Korean intelligence officers in a number of ways, including sharing with them notes she had prepared for a meeting in 2022 between top State Department officials and Korea policy experts. She also admitted accepting designer handbags valued at more than $9,200, 19 meals at fine restaurants and $37,000 in payments to a public policy program on Korean affairs that she ran, as gifts from South Korean intelligence officers. Born in Seoul and raised in Virginia, Terry was a senior CIA analyst from 2001 to 2008, and director of Korean, Japan and Oceanic Affairs at the NSC from 2008 to 2009 under Republican President George W. Bush and Democratic President Barack Obama.

item.title: US Justice Department threatens California over alleged noncitizen voters, letters show
item.description: The US Justice Department on Tuesday gave California officials 48 hours to review a list of alleged noncitizen voters or face legal action, according to two letters reviewed by Reuters, part of an unprecedented effort to find evidence of voter fraud ahead of next month's elections.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Bogage , Andrew Goudsward
item.content:encoded: The US Justice Department on Tuesday gave California officials 48 hours to review a list of alleged noncitizen voters or face legal action, according to two letters reviewed by Reuters, part of an unprecedented effort to find evidence of voter fraud ahead of next month's elections . The letters, written by acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter and addressed to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan, say the Justice Department provided officials in Los Angeles County with a "password-protected thumb drive" with the names of people the federal government "believes are likely noncitizens" and were sent mail-in ballots from California. The letters demand that the state and county segregate returned mail-in ballots from voters on the Justice Department's list and not tabulate their votes "until citizenship has been determined." In cases where ballots have not been sent out yet, it orders California officials to withhold them from those on the list until their citizenship is confirmed. The federal government "will have no choice but to seek emergency relief," according to the letters, if state and county officials do not follow its instructions. "Allowing noncitizens to vote cancels citizen votes," McCotter wrote. The letters mark an escalation of the Trump administration's attempts to pressure states over alleged voting by non-US citizens and signal the Justice Department may be prepared to challenge ballots in the weeks leading up to the November 3 election, when Republicans will be defending their narrow majorities in Congress. Justice Department spokeswoman Kiersten Pels confirmed the existence of the letters in a statement to Reuters, adding: "The department will take all necessary legal action to protect election integrity and ensure compliance with federal law.” Representatives from the White House and the California secretary of state's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Logan also did not immediately respond. FRAUD CLAIMS The Justice Department under President Donald Trump has repeatedly claimed that voting by non-US citizens is widespread, despite multiple studies showing it is rare. Though states may have added more than [USN:L6N43Z058 TEXT:"30,000 noncitizens to their voter rolls"] since 2000 due to software glitches and clerical errors, Reuters found in September, it was unclear how many had cast a ballot. Experts said the numbers were too small relative to the country’s 170 million registered voters to affect elections. In July, the Justice Department [USN:L6N43A182 TEXT:"sent letters"] to chief election officials in all 50 states warning they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls or cast ballots. The department's Civil Rights Division has demanded nonpublic voter data, including voters' Social Security numbers or dates of birth, from nearly all states as part of its hunt for noncitizens on state rolls. It has [USN:L6N44118V TEXT:"sued"] 30 Democratic- and Republican-led states that refused to hand over their rolls, but has [USN:S0N3R907R TEXT:"lost 26 of those cases"] without winning one. Reuters [USN:L6N45D0T4 TEXT:"reported"] last month that the Department of Homeland Security was using a commercial data broker to find sensitive voter information not included in publicly available rolls, which officials and experts warned could lead to citizens being falsely flagged as illegal voters and potentially detained. Federal prosecutors have also [USN:L6N45F10R TEXT:"ramped up"] prosecutions of noncitizens for allegedly voting in past elections or submitting fraudulent registrations, touting 16 new criminal cases on Monday. Officials in Democratic-led California have tussled for months with the Trump administration over its attempts to intervene in election procedures over allegations of voter fraud. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin informed California officials on July 16 that the federal government believed the state had noncitizens on its voting rolls, according to the letter. California could prove pivotal in deciding control of the US House of Representatives, especially after the state's voters approved a new congressional map that heavily favors Democrats as part of a nationwide redistricting sprint that began in Republican-led states. Voters in Los Angeles will also weigh in on a ballot measure that would allow certain noncitizen legal residents to cast ballots in municipal elections.

item.title: Gold drops over 1% as hot US inflation data boosts Fed hike bets
item.description: Gold fell over 1% on Wednesday, extending losses for a third straight session, as a stronger-than-expected inflation reading increased US Federal Reserve rate-hike bets for this month.
item.dc:creator: Pablo Sinha
item.content:encoded: Gold fell over 1% on Wednesday, extending losses for a third straight session, as a stronger-than-expected inflation reading increased US Federal Reserve rate-hike bets for this month. Spot gold dropped 1.8% to $4,083.94 per ounce by 2:05 p.m. EDT (1805 GMT), its lowest since October 7. US gold futures for December delivery settled 1.7% lower at $4,107.90 per ounce. The US dollar index (.DXY) climbed 0.5%, making greenback-denominated gold more expensive for holders of other currencies, while 10-year US Treasury yields also rose. "At this point it portends that the Fed is more likely to raise interest rates," David Meger, director of metals trading at High Ridge Futures, said, citing hotter-than-expected consumer price index (CPI) data that has remained above Fed targets. "As a result, we've seen the dollar rise and pressure added to the gold market." [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"The CPI"] rose 0.6% last month after climbing 0.4% in August, the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics said on Wednesday. Markets see about a 42% chance of a US rate hike this month, up from about 22% before the inflation data, and are pricing in a 93% probability of an increase in December, according to CME's FedWatch Tool . While gold is typically seen as a hedge against inflation, higher interest rates tend to diminish the appeal of non-yielding bullion. Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said the central bank has time to [USN:L1N4600EO TEXT:"wait and see"] how financial markets and the economy evolve after its September rate rise before deciding whether to take any more action. Oil prices rose on Wednesday after an attack on the headquarters of Saudi Arabia's state-owned oil company, while Iranian officials told Reuters they were deploying new tactics to target ships, seeking to keep oil prices high and influence US midterm elections. "In the longer term, gold should again benefit from continued strong central-bank buying and renewed concerns over US debt and its rising interest burden," said Julius Baer analyst Carsten Menke. Among other metals, spot silver fell 6.6% to $55.53 per ounce, platinum dipped 3.5% to $1,605.37 per ounce and palladium fell 2.8% to $1,094.50 per ounce.

item.title: Stocks fall, dollar rallies as US inflation tops forecasts
item.description: The dollar rose while Wall Street stocks fell on Wednesday after data showed US consumer prices rose more than expected last month, reinforcing expectations the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates as soon as this month.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Cooper, Chibuike Oguh
item.content:encoded: The dollar rose while Wall Street stocks fell on Wednesday after data showed US consumer prices rose more than expected last month, reinforcing expectations the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates as soon as this month. US Labor Department [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"data showed"] the core consumer price index up 0.3% in September versus economist expectations for a rise of 0.2%. On an annual basis, core CPI, which strips out food and energy prices, rose 2.6%, above forecasts for a rise of 2.5%, while the headline rate rose 3.7%, above estimates for a rise of 3.6%. The dollar rose 0.36% against a basket of currencies to its highest since April 2025, while US 2-year Treasury yields , which are most sensitive to shifts in expectations for inflation and monetary policy, leapt 0.23 basis point on the day to 4.87%. "The reading was hotter than expected, not just with energy but elsewhere, suggesting higher tariffs and conflict-driven disruptions are bleeding into other categories," said Mark Hackett, chief market strategist at Nationwide. "Investors are coming to terms with 'higher-for-longer' inflation." Money markets showed traders upped their bets on the chances of the Federal Reserve delivering another rate rise this month to around 41%, from closer to 20% prior to the data , while cementing the odds of an additional rise in December, according to LSEG data. The euro dropped 0.4% to $1.1153, while the pound fell 0.53% to $1.3182. The Japanese yen was at 158.16 per dollar. STOCKS FALL On Wall Street, all three indexes were trading lower with technology and industrials driving losses while healthcare, consumer staples and energy stocks were higher. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) fell 0.37%, the S&P 500 (.SPX) fell 1.33% and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) fell 2.14%. More of Wall Street's big banks reported earnings, with [USN:L4N4600XY TEXT:"Bank of America"], which saw profits fall in the third quarter, and [USN:L4N46010U TEXT:"Morgan Stanley"] (MS.N) , which beat expectations for its third-quarter profit thanks to strong equity trading. Europe's STOXX 600 (.STOXX) pared some of the day's gains and finished up 0.43%, while the MSCI All-World index (.MIWD00000PUS) fell 0.96%. Sentiment was already fragile prior to the consumer data, given the renewed strength in oil prices following attacks on two vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and after Iranian officials told Reuters they were deploying [USN:L8N45Z15J TEXT:"new tactics"] to target ships, raising the risk of fresh disruption to energy supplies. Brent crude futures , which are around their highest in nearly two weeks, rose 0.35% to settle at $106.06 a barrel. Spot gold fell 1.49% to $4,094.88 an ounce.

item.title: Oil prices gain on attacks in Saudi Arabia, Iran's new tactics to target tankers
item.description: Oil prices rose on Wednesday after the Houthis attacked Saudi Aramco's headquarters and Iran said it was deploying new tactics to target ships and keep oil prices high.
item.dc:creator: Nicole Jao
item.content:encoded: Oil prices rose on Wednesday after the Houthis attacked Saudi Aramco's headquarters and Iran said it was deploying [USN:L8N45Z15J TEXT:"new tactics"] to target ships and keep oil prices high. Brent crude futures were up 87 cents, or 0.82%, at $106.56 a barrel by 1:25 p.m. ET (1725 GMT). US West Texas Intermediate crude gained $1.46, or 1.55%, to $95.60, touching a three-week high. Attacks on ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz and strikes between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-allied Houthis are driving up oil prices, said Phil Flynn, senior analyst with the Price Futures Group. "We're seeing a lot of fear trade today," he added. Iranian officials declined to provide details of the new strategy to target ships, but one said Iran had started using different offensive tactics about 10 days ago. Gulf oil flows excluding Iran surged in September to more than 81% of prewar levels, data showed, led by a recovery in Saudi exports. Iranian exports fell to zero owing to a US blockade. "More crude reaching international markets does not necessarily mean more oil is being produced," Saxo Bank analyst Ole Hansen said in a note. "Some of the recovery reflects a redistribution of available barrels, including volumes that would otherwise have supplied regional refineries." ATTACKS ON MULTIPLE FRONTS The Houthis [USN:L6N4600QH TEXT:"attacked "]an administrative building belonging to state-owned oil company Saudi Aramco (2222.SE) in the city of Dhahran, causing a limited fire, Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said. The group has fired ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia over the past week in what it says is retaliation for the kingdom's support of Yemeni government forces. Riyadh's [USN:L6N45Y0C1 TEXT:"international airport"] has been hit four times, with a strike on Saturday killing 13 people. Meanwhile, a [USN:S8N43Z00E TEXT:"container ship sank"] in waters south of the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a naval mine and catching fire, Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said in a statement shared by state media on Wednesday. This was a day after the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said a container ship and a tanker were hit by unknown projectiles within the strait. "The expectation that increased Russian diesel exports will ease market tightness is likely to limit sharp price movement in either direction," said Hiroyuki Kikukawa, chief strategist at Nissan Securities Investment. US President Donald Trump announced on Friday that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian diesel that were designed to deprive Moscow of revenue for its war in Ukraine . Russia's crude oil [USN:L1N46008R TEXT:"production increased"] by 65,000 barrels per day in September to 8.43 million bpd but remained down 870,000 bpd year over year, the International Energy Agency said on Wednesday. The IEA also said a lack of operational Russian refinery capacity meant that the recently announced easing of Russian diesel export restrictions was unlikely to bring any material change to the global gasoil market balance. Constrained diesel supplies could persist well into next year, the IEA said. The oil market was watching for weekly storage reports from the American Petroleum Institute trade group on Wednesday and the US Energy Information Administration on Thursday, a day later than usual due to a holiday on Monday.

item.title: Zelenskiy receives full-throated UK support after Trump turns on him
item.description: Volodymyr Zelenskiy received a strong show of support in London on Wednesday, meeting Prime Minister Andy Burnham and King Charles after the Ukrainian leader's relationship with the US took a sharp turn for the worse.
item.dc:creator: William James
item.content:encoded: Volodymyr Zelenskiy received a strong show of support in London on Wednesday, meeting Prime Minister Andy Burnham and King Charles after the Ukrainian leader's relationship with the US took a sharp turn for the worse. Zelenskiy was given the red-carpet treatment, arriving in Britain after another night of heavy Russian attacks and hours after [USN:L8N4600M6 TEXT:"Ukraine accused Elon Musk's SpaceX"] of crippling its drones by limiting Starlink services. The diplomatic display, which included a 25-minute audience with Charles and a ceremonial guard in Downing Street, echoed Zelenskiy's February 2025 visit to London shortly after he had clashed with US President Donald Trump and his deputy JD Vance. At the start of Wednesday's Downing Street meeting, Zelenskiy said he wanted to discuss the difficulties over Starlink and intelligence sharing, and that Ukraine still relied on its partnership with the United States. Trump said at the weekend Zelenskiy [USN:L6N45W06G TEXT:"should be replaced"] as Ukraine's leader, days after he cut a deal with Moscow to [USN:L4N45Y0AR TEXT:"lift sanctions"] on Russian diesel exports. Britain has said it does not support the US-Russia diesel deal, and called for allies to keep up the economic pressure on Moscow. In an interview with broadcaster Piers Morgan, Zelenskiy said it was [USN:L8N46022D TEXT:"painful when Trump sided with Russia"] over Ukraine. Burnham said the last few days had been "very dark and difficult" for Ukraine, but that Britain remained a staunch ally. "We're behind you, and that will not change," he said. Earlier he announced the planned delivery of £45 million ($59.60 million) of surface-to-air missiles used to target jet-powered Russian drones, with £10 million of that package fast-tracked to meet an urgent need in Ukraine. Burnham has asked officials to draw up further sanctions, military aid, and fiscal support, and his foreign and finance ministers have been lobbying allies to follow Britain in banning maritime services that support Russian liquefied natural gas exports. ($1 = 0.7551 pounds)

item.title: US banks post solid third-quarter loan growth, but face more competition for deposits
item.description: US banks reported solid loan and deposit growth in the third quarter, but lenders are paying a premium to retain customer funds in a fiercely competitive, high-interest-rate environment.
item.dc:creator: Pritam Biswas, Prakhar Srivastava
item.content:encoded: US banks reported solid loan and deposit growth in the third quarter, but lenders are paying a premium to retain customer funds in a fiercely competitive, high-interest-rate environment. JPMorgan Chase (JPM.N) , Citigroup (C.N) and Wells Fargo (WFC.N) all posted higher net interest income on Tuesday, even as investors worried that soaring bond yields and elevated borrowing costs would stifle loan demand and trigger a flight of deposits. Bank of America (BAC.N) , the second-largest US lender, also reported higher net interest income on Wednesday. "The economic uncertainty that prevails and the geopolitical instability are always present, but what our clients are actually doing is continuing to point to a resilient and growing economy in the United States," Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan said on a conference call with analysts. Citigroup reported an 11% increase in average deposits and a 12% jump in average loans. Wells Fargo said average deposits rose 10.7%, alongside an 11% jump in average loans buoyed by its consumer banking division. JPMorgan, the largest US lender, reported a 4% rise in average deposits and a 2% increase in loans from a year ago. Bank of America's average deposits rose 2% in the third quarter while average loans and leases grew 6% over the year-ago period. Despite resilient metrics, banks face mounting funding pressures. As US Treasury yields jumped in the third quarter, customers sought better returns elsewhere, forcing lenders to raise deposit rates to prevent outflows and squeezing their margins. This was exemplified by JPMorgan's deposit margin that fell to 2.78% in the third quarter from 2.79% in the year-ago period and Wells Fargo's net interest margin on a taxable basis that slumped to 2.43% in the reported quarter from 2.61% a year earlier. "Loan and deposit growth continue to chug along, albeit maybe with some concern on deposits," said Truist analyst Brian Foran. POTENTIAL CREDIT LOSSES IN FOCUS So far, analysts said there have been no significant cracks in overall bank credit quality, suggesting households have continued to manage their debt obligations. A weakening labor market and rising living costs could pressure borrowers, especially if prolonged conflicts drive up prices for essential goods and squeeze discretionary spending. Despite concerns that rising consumer spending is merely a reflection of inflation crowding out non-essential purchases, internal data does not show consumers shifting away from discretionary items, JPMorgan Chief Financial Officer Jeremy Barnum said on a call with analysts. US consumer prices [USN:L1N452123 TEXT:"rose 3.4% in the 12 months through August"], matching July's increase, while a measure of underlying inflation posted its largest monthly gain in four months. [USN:L1N45N170 TEXT:"US job growth"] slowed more than expected in September. Sharp downward revisions to payrolls in previous months added to uncertainty about the economic outlook and the potential strength of future loan demand. Wells Fargo and Citigroup increased their provisions for credit losses in the third quarter, a trend the other banks might soon follow in the current macroeconomic landscape. In September, major US banks [USN:L4N4581DW TEXT:"raised their prime lending rates"] following the Federal Reserve rate hike that raised borrowing costs for consumers and businesses.

item.title: As EU debates local-content rules, Chinese automakers are already adapting
item.description: As Europe debates new local-content rules aimed at boosting local manufacturing, Chinese automakers are already building factories and supply chains across the continent, getting ahead of the measures before they have even been finalised.
item.dc:creator: Nick Carey, Rachel More
item.content:encoded: As Europe debates new local-content rules aimed at boosting local manufacturing, Chinese automakers are already building factories and supply chains across the continent, getting ahead of the measures before they have even been finalised. The European Union's proposed "Made in Europe" rules, part of a planned Industrial Accelerator Act, are designed to strengthen the bloc's industrial base by encouraging more manufacturing and sourcing within Europe. The measures would also push foreign manufacturers seeking access to the EU market to produce more goods locally and rely on European suppliers. The plan comes as Chinese automakers have rapidly gained market share in Europe, with more entrants on the way. But "Made in Europe" has sparked a political dispute within Europe over which countries should be covered by the rules. Many Chinese automakers, meanwhile, appear unwilling to wait for the outcome. Pressing ahead with localisation plans, they are expanding manufacturing and supplier networks in Europe before the details of any new requirements are settled. Battered by an EV price war and slowing sales in China, the world's largest auto market, Chinese automakers increasingly see Europe as a key growth opportunity. "We are committed to building our local production capacity and exploring opportunities here," Changan Automobile (000625.SZ) Zhao Fei told reporters at the Paris car show. Zhao said he had already visited Europe twice for "in-depth discussions" with suppliers and was also talking to European automakers about producing vehicles together. Changan plans to make 180,000 cars a year in Europe by 2028 and 350,000 by 2030, The company's president said he hopes Changan can build its first vehicle in Europe by the middle of 2027, well before any EU local-content requirements are expected to take effect. Other Chinese automakers, including Xpeng (9868.HK) , Chery (9973.HK) and GAC (601238.SS) , are also pursuing European production plans built around local supply bases. "We're looking to start production at the same time" as 'Made in Europe' rules take effect, Xpeng Vice President Yeqing Zheng said of plans to add production capacity in Europe. Magna (MG.TO) already builds EVs for Xpeng in Austria. Some industry experts argue Chinese automakers are moving faster than EU policymakers, raising questions about how much impact the final rules will have. John Bozzella, CEO of US auto industry lobby group Alliance for Automotive Innovation, said Europe is viewed as a "cautionary tale" in the US for acting too late in response to Chinese competition. The US Senate is working to pass a bill [USN:L1N45G0S2 TEXT:"permanently banning "]Chinese cars, which Bozzella said reflects concerns over data security. "The policy responses seem to be happening in response to market realities in Europe," he said. "But in the US all sides are saying, 'let's try and address these issues up front.'" 'WE GREW TOGETHER' In a speech at the Paris motor show, Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume [USN:L6N45X048 TEXT:"backed"] 'Made in Europe', saying "a strong Europe depends on a strong industry". But in its current form, the proposal excludes non-EU countries such as Turkey, Britain and Morocco, where vehicle production and supplier networks are deeply integrated with Europe's automotive industry. Automakers with operations in those countries, along with local industry groups, argue that limiting the definition of Europe to the EU would damage supply chains that have developed across the wider region. Turkey's Automotive Industry Exporters' Association (OIB) says the country's automotive industry supports 250,000 EU jobs. More than 50% of the parts by value in Ford's (F.N) Turkish-made electric Transit vans come from EU suppliers, including batteries from Hungary and Poland and components from Germany, Italy and elsewhere. "We grew together," said OIB chairman Kemal Yazici. "Turkey is an integral part of Europe's" auto industry. Alongside drafting local content rules, the EU has also brokered [USN:L6N45V0LF TEXT:"a deal"] with China to more than halve hybrid vehicle imports into the bloc. When asked about the deal, Chery (9973.HK) Chairman Yin Tongyue told Reuters the company would first study the details. But he was more interested in discussing Chery's plans for Europe. "We want to design locally," Yin said. "We want to have local engineering, local production and a local supply chain." Automotive analyst Felipe Munoz said Chinese automakers were unlikely to be deterred by the policy debate as they have demonstrated an ability to "do anything, very fast". When the EU imposed tariffs on Chinese-made EVs in October 2024, many shifted their focus to tariff-free plug-in hybrids. 'Made in Europe' is "making life a bit more difficult for the Chinese," Munoz said. "But it won't stop them."
